Question 4 [10 marks]: How does the study of public buildings help historians understand society in Pompeii and Herculaneum? Support your response using evidence from Sources D and E and other relevant sources.

MARKING CRITERIA (out of 10):
9–10 marks: Provides a well-developed and informed explanation of how the study of public buildings helps historians understand society in Pompeii and Herculaneum | Integrates evidence from Sources D and E and other relevant sources to support the response | Uses a range of appropriate historical terms and concepts
7–8 marks: Provides an informed explanation of how the study of public buildings helps historians understand society in Pompeii and Herculaneum | Uses evidence from Sources D and E and other relevant source(s) to support the response | Uses appropriate historical terms and concepts
5–6 marks: Provides some explanation of how the study of public buildings helps historians understand society in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum | Refers to Sources D and E and may refer to other source(s) | Uses some appropriate historical terms and concepts
3–4 marks: Provides some description of how public buildings help historians understand society in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum | Refers to Source D and/or Source E and/or other source(s) | May use historical terms and/or concepts
1–2 marks: Makes general statement(s) about public buildings in Pompeii and/or Herculaneum | May refer to Source D and/or Source E and/or other source(s)


ANSWERS COULD INCLUDE (the student does not need every point):
• Public buildings in Pompeii and Herculaneum help historians understand much about society, such as its stratified nature, religious beliefs and practices, political and economic life.
Source D
• The Pompeiian forum demonstrates that public buildings were often centralised
• The Macellum provides information regarding the economic life of Pompeii
• The Temple of Vespasian (Genius of Augustus) demonstrates the imperial influence on religion
• The Building of Eumachia reveals the influence of women on public life.
Source E
• Evidence for public buildings at Herculaneum, despite a lack of excavation, reveals that the town had a thriving public life which was influenced by imperial Rome
• Written evidence for the missing Macellum reveals the importance of political patronage
• The existence of temples, such as the Temple of Jupiter, reveals the importance of public religion.
Other sources
• Inscriptions on public buildings indicate political patronage
• Baths, amphitheatres and palaestrae indicate the importance of leisure activities and social stratification
• Municipal buildings, such as the Basilica, demonstrate the administrative practices.
